title: A Roadside Stand
summary: Robert Frost describes a small stand set up by poor rural folk beside a highway, where they hope to sell berries and squash to passing city motorists. The cars rush by indifferently, and the poet feels the pain of the villagers’ unfulfilled hopes, criticises the hollow promises of so-called benefactors, and reflects on the deep divide between the rich city and the neglected countryside.

notes.heading: About the poet
notes.html: Robert Frost (1874–1963) was an American poet who won four Pulitzer Prizes. His poems, set in rural New England, use simple language to explore deep human and philosophical questions.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: A little old shed has been extended into a roadside stand by poor farmers who want a share of the city’s money. Speeding cars pass without stopping; the few who do stop only ask for directions, buy petrol, or complain that the painted signs spoil the landscape. The poet sympathises with the farmers who wait all day for a car to halt. He mocks the greedy good-doers who promise to relocate the farmers to villages near theatres and shops, only to take away their independence. He ends feeling so overwhelmed by their sorrow that he wishes, for a moment, to end their pain at once, and then questions how he would feel if someone did that to him.

notes.heading: Stanza-wise explanation (paraphrase)
notes.html:
Stanza 1: The stand and the passing traffic. An old shed has been pushed out to the edge of the road to become a stand. The owners are not begging; they want a little city money to support their lives, as rightful earning. The motorists, however, rush past, fixed on their destinations. If anyone glances at the stand, it is only to criticise that its crude, hand-painted signs spoil the view. The farmers display wild berries in wooden cups and golden crook-necked squash with silver warts, and a beautiful mountain scene, but the city people do not care. The poet says that the farmers ought to have city money flowing to them, but it does not.

Stanza 2: The hollow promises. The poet has heard of plans to buy out the farmers and settle them in villages near the theatre and the shop, where they will be relieved of thinking for themselves. These benefactors, whom he calls greedy good-doers and beneficent beasts of prey, pretend to help but actually exploit them. They will teach them to sleep the day away, destroying their peace and independence.

Stanza 3: The waiting. The poet finds it hard to bear the farmers’ childlike longing as they sit at the window all day, hoping for the sound of a car stopping. Occasionally a car does stop, but only to turn around or ask the way, or to ask whether they sell gasoline.

Stanza 4: The poet’s anguish. Moved by their misery, the poet half-wishes their pain could be ended all at once. But he catches himself: if someone came to end his own pain in such a way, he would not like it. The ending shows his deep compassion and the complexity of the situation.

notes.heading: Poetic devices
notes.html:
• Irony and sarcasm: calling exploiters ‘good-doers’ and beasts of prey who are ‘beneficent’.
  • Oxymoron: the pairing of ‘greedy’ with ‘good-doers’ and ‘beneficent’ with ‘beasts of prey’.
  • Imagery: wooden cups of berries, crook-necked squash with silver warts.
  • Personification: the stand ‘pleading’ for city money; the landscape that can be ‘marred’.
  • Alliteration: repeated consonant sounds, e.g. in the description of the squash.
  • Rhyme scheme: generally rhyming lines, though irregular.
  • Contrast: wealthy city versus impoverished countryside.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Rural–urban divide: indifference of affluent city dwellers to the poor rural people.
  • Exploitation disguised as welfare: hollow promises of politicians and planners.
  • Dignity of labour: the farmers want to earn, not beg.
  • Compassion and helplessness: the poet’s sympathy and his inability to help.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The roadside stand is the central image of the poem, representing the hopes and struggles of the rural poor at the edge of a prosperous world that passes them by. The title therefore captures both the setting and the theme.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Development must include the rural poor. We should treat them with respect, buy from them fairly and support genuine welfare, not exploitation dressed as charity.

keyTerms.definition: A small temporary stall by a road where local farmers sell produce.
A vegetable of the gourd family; the farmers sell golden crook-necked squash.
Ironic term for those who pretend to help but exploit the poor.
Oxymoronic description of exploiters who appear kind but devour the weak.
Spoiled; motorists complain that the signs mar the landscape.
Two contradictory words placed together for effect.
Saying the opposite of what is meant, used to criticise the benefactors.
Economic and social gap between villages and cities.

mcqs.q: What did the farmers want from the roadside stand?
options: A share of city money through sales
mcqs.explanation: They wanted to earn some city money by selling produce, not to beg.

mcqs.q: How do most city motorists react to the stand?
options: They rush past without noticing, or only complain.
mcqs.explanation: The cars speed by indifferently; those who look only complain about the signs.

mcqs.q: What complaint do some passers-by make?
options: The painted signs spoil the landscape.
mcqs.explanation: They grumble that the crude signs mar the scenery.

mcqs.q: What items are sold at the stand?
mcqs.explanation: The farmers sell wild berries in wooden cups and golden squash, along with offering the scenic view.

options: Exploiters, such as politicians and planners, who pretend to help
mcqs.explanation: The phrase describes so-called benefactors who exploit the poor while claiming to help.

mcqs.q: What do the ‘good-doers’ plan for the farmers?
options: To buy them out and resettle them near theatres and stores
mcqs.explanation: They plan to relocate them to villages near theatres and shops, taking away their independence.

mcqs.q: Why does a car occasionally stop at the stand?
options: To ask the way or turn around, or to ask for gasoline
mcqs.explanation: Cars stop only to ask directions, turn around or ask if gas is sold.

mcqs.q: The expression ‘beneficent beasts of prey’ is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: ‘Beneficent’ and ‘beasts of prey’ are contradictory, forming an oxymoron (with alliteration too).

mcqs.q: What thought does the poet have at the end of the poem?
options: He wants to open a shop.
He momentarily wishes to end the farmers’ pain at once, then questions it.
He decides to move to the city.
mcqs.explanation: Overwhelmed, he wishes to end their pain in one stroke, but realises he would not want that for himself.

mcqs.q: The main theme of the poem is:
options: The indifference of the urban rich to the rural poor
mcqs.explanation: Frost highlights the rural–urban divide and the neglect of the poor.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: The poet describes how the farmers sit by the window all day, longing with an almost childlike hope to hear a car slow down and stop at their stand.
(a) Why do the farmers wait so eagerly? (1)
(b) What usually happens when a car stops? (1)
(c) What does ‘childlike’ suggest about their hope? (1)
(d) What is the poet’s feeling towards them? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) They hope to sell their produce and earn some money.

(b) It stops only to ask the way, turn around or ask for gasoline.

(c) Their hope is innocent, simple and repeatedly disappointed.

(d) Deep sympathy and pain.

questions.q: What is the grievance of the city people against the roadside stand?
questions.answerHtml: The city people feel that the crude, hand-painted signboards of the stand spoil the beauty of the landscape. Instead of buying anything, they criticise the stand, showing their insensitivity to the struggles of the rural poor.

questions.q: Why does the poet call the benefactors ‘greedy good-doers’?
questions.answerHtml: They pretend to work for the welfare of the rural poor by promising to resettle them in better villages. But in reality they serve their own selfish interests and take away the farmers’ independence. Hence the poet calls them greedy good-doers, an ironic oxymoron.

questions.q: What does the poet wish at the end of the poem, and why does he reconsider?
questions.answerHtml: Unable to bear the farmers’ misery, the poet momentarily wishes their pain could be ended all at once. He reconsiders because he imagines how he himself would feel if someone tried to end his pain that way; he would not like it.

questions.q: How does ‘A Roadside Stand’ highlight the contrast between the rural poor and the urban rich? (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Frost’s poem draws a sharp contrast between two worlds. The rural folk are poor and hardworking. They extend an old shed into a roadside stand and display wild berries and golden squash, hoping to earn a little money for a better life. They do not beg; they want a fair share of the wealth that flows through the cities.

The urban rich, in contrast, are self-absorbed. They speed past in cars, eyes fixed on their destinations. If they notice the stand, it is only to complain that its signs spoil the view. The few who stop want directions or fuel, not produce.

The poet also exposes the false sympathy of planners and politicians who promise to resettle the poor near theatres and shops but actually exploit them. Through this contrast, Frost criticises the indifference of prosperity and pleads for genuine respect and support for the countryside.

questions.q: Discuss the poet’s attitude towards the farmers in ‘A Roadside Stand’. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
The poet’s attitude towards the farmers is one of deep sympathy and respect. He stresses that they are not beggars asking for charity; they want to earn honest money by selling their berries and squash. He respects this dignity of labour.

He feels their pain intensely. Watching them sit all day by the window, hoping a car will stop, he finds their childlike longing almost unbearable. Each car that stops only to turn around or ask for gas deepens their disappointment, and his.

He is angry on their behalf at the so-called good-doers who promise them a better life but plan to uproot them and make them dependent. His sarcasm shows his protectiveness.

At the end, his compassion becomes so strong that he wishes their suffering could end at once, but he checks himself, realising they too have pride and choice. His attitude is thus tender, sensitive and humane.
